newsitem.title: USA: U.S. officials warn consumers about fake solicitors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials warn consumers about fake solicitors.

text.p: The government and all 50 state attorneys general warned consumers Wednesday to be wary of for-profit fundraisers who claim to be police officers or firefighters.

"Badge-related fraud is a multi-billion dollar illegal enterprise that preys on people's trust in their local police and fire departments," Jodie Bernstein, director of the Federal Trade Commission's bureau of consumer affairs, told a news conference. She said consumers asked to donate money on behalf of law enforcement should call their local police or fire departments to verify who gets the cash.

In a warning called "Operation False Alarm" the FTC said a caller claiming to be a police officer should "raise red flags for consumers because in many states and locales police are prohibited by law or department policy from soliciting donations."
Several attorneys general said such operations were widespread.

"We were surprised at the magnitude and sophistication of this fraudulent operation," Ohio Attorney General Betty Montgomery said. "We found businesses in almost every county of Ohio that lost money through these scams."

Often a business agreed to purchase an ad from a magazine under the false impression it had a connection to legitimate law enforcement. Beyond that, the magazine was not distributed to the community -- as claimed -- so the business failed to get a benefit from the ad.

To add insult to injury the business was often billed repeatedly for more ads, whether or not they were authorised, and then hounded to pay the bills with the threat the bill would be turned over to a collection agency.
"Use extreme caution when giving money over the phone or through the mail for journals that are supposed to educate the public about drug awareness or fire safety," Montgomery said.

In one case, Leon Saja of Phoenix, Arizona, doing business as Southwest Publishing, fraudulently solicited donations on behalf of such groups as the "American Deputy Sheriff's Association" and "United Fire Fighters Association," the FTC said. The government obtained a court order against Saja and froze his assets.

In another case the government cracked down on Southwest Marketing Concepts, also known as "The Journal -- the Voice of Law Enforcement." Telemarketers sold the journal as a way to help fight drugs and crime.
The FTC said the company falsely charged companies for advertising whether or not it was authorised and threatened their credit ratings if they failed to pay.

The FTC and the National Association of Attorneys General recommended consumers ask for written information from any supposed charity and watch out for names that closely resemble those of respected, legitimate organisations. They also suggested refusing high pressure appeals.

Finally, they recommended making an annual plan for giving. "Identify the causes you want to support and then do your homework by checking out the charities that support those causes," they said. "Don't stop giving."
